title: Number Hunt Outdoors
strapline: Maths is everywhere outside — go and find it.
intent: Taking maths outdoors makes it big, physical and real — counting, comparing and matching with the whole body and the whole world.
Hunting for numbers, quantities and shapes turns abstract number into an exciting treasure hunt.
Collecting and comparing natural objects is genuine counting, sorting and measuring with a purpose.
Movement and maths together suit children who learn best on the move and struggle to sit still.
The outdoors is full of real number talk — how many, how far, which is bigger, one each.
implementation: Hide or chalk numerals around the garden and set children off to find, name and match them.
Turn collecting into counting: find me three leaves, the same number of stones as your fingers, something for everyone.
Model number talk in real situations: 'How many are we? So how many cups do we need?'
Compare and measure with natural things: whose stick is longer, which bucket holds more, sort the conkers by size.
Add numerals, tens frames or number tracks outdoors so children match quantity to symbol.
Weave counting into physical play: jump five times, run to number four, hop as many times as the dice.
Follow real problems as they arise — sharing the snack, lining up the trikes, scoring a game.
key_questions: How many can you find — can you count them out loud?
Which is more, and how can we check?
Can you find the number four — what does it look like?
How can we share these fairly so everyone gets some?
How could we measure which one is longer?

impact.text: Children count objects with one-to-one correspondence and growing accuracy.
Children recognise and name numerals and match them to the right quantity.
Children compare amounts, sizes and distances using 'more', 'fewer', 'longer' and 'the same'.
Children subitise small groups — seeing how many without counting — during the hunt.
Children use number physically — jumping, running and hopping set amounts.
Children talk through their counting and comparing, explaining how they know.

enhancements: Chalked or hidden numerals and number tracks around the outdoor area.
Baskets and buckets for collecting and counting natural treasures.
Number tiles, tens frames and large dice for outdoor number games.
Balance scales, buckets and string for comparing and measuring.
A giant number line or hopscotch painted on the ground.
A trolley of loose parts — stones, cones, sticks — for endless counting and sorting.

playing_exploring: Children hunt, collect and explore number in the real, physical world.
They test quantities and sizes with their own hands and bodies.
active_learning: Children stay with a counting or comparing challenge, driven by the fun of the hunt.
creating_thinking: Children work out how many, how much and how to share, and explain their reasoning.
